name: Boyle's Law
statement: At constant temperature, a gas's pressure rises as its volume falls.
statementAccent: pressure rises as its volume falls
meaning: Squeeze a fixed amount of gas into half the space, at unchanged temperature, and its pressure doubles; let it expand to twice the volume and the pressure halves. Pressure and volume trade off so that their product stays constant.
mechanism: Gas pressure comes from molecules striking the container walls. Shrink the volume and the same molecules are packed into a smaller space, so they hit the walls more often per unit area and the pressure rises. Because temperature is held constant, molecular speed does not change — it is the collision frequency, not harder hits, that varies.

examples.text: Block a syringe's nozzle and push the plunger: the trapped gas's volume drops and its pressure climbs; pull back and pressure falls — a direct demonstration of the inverse relationship.
The diaphragm enlarges the chest cavity, increasing lung volume so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric, and air flows in; exhaling reverses it. Boyle's law made mechanical.
As a diver rises, the surrounding water pressure drops, so a fixed amount of gas in the lungs expands — the reason divers are warned never to hold their breath while ascending.

variants.name: Mariotte's law
variants.text: The same law under its continental European name, after Edme Mariotte, who found it independently around 1679 and added that it holds at constant temperature.

variants.name: The ideal gas law
variants.text: Boyle's law is the constant-temperature, fixed-amount slice of PV = nRT, the unified relation that also contains Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, and Avogadro's laws.

whyItMatters: It was among the first quantitative laws of gas behaviour and a founding result of physical chemistry, the pressure-volume relationship that underlies everything from syringes and lungs to the design of pressure vessels. It is also a clean component of the ideal gas law, into which it and its sibling laws assemble.

working.text: the inverse relationship applies only to a sealed, fixed quantity of gas at constant temperature; changing either breaks it.
since pressure times volume stays constant, use P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ to find one state from another.
at high pressure or low temperature, treat the law as approximate and reach for a real-gas correction.

limits: Boyle's law holds only for an ideal gas, at constant temperature and fixed amount. Real gases deviate, especially at high pressure and low temperature, where molecular volume and intermolecular attractions matter — deviations described by the van der Waals equation and the compressibility factor. It is an accurate approximation within its regime and a limiting-case idealisation outside it.
misreadings: It is not an exact universal law but an ideal-gas approximation, and it says nothing when temperature or the amount of gas changes. The attribution is also shared: Richard Towneley and Henry Power noted the pressure-volume relationship just before Boyle confirmed it, and Mariotte found it independently, so 'Boyle's law' honours a contributor rather than a sole discoverer.
origin: Published by the Anglo-Irish natural philosopher Robert Boyle in 1662, in a defence of his air-pump work, after Richard Towneley and Henry Power had noted the relationship (the 'Towneley hypothesis') and with experimental help from Robert Hooke. Edme Mariotte found it independently around 1679, hence 'Mariotte's law' in much of Europe.

sources.text: Boyle's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the kinetic mechanism, the Towneley/Power/Mariotte attributions, and the real-gas limits.
Boyle's law, New World Encyclopedia. — Mariotte's independent 1679 discovery.
